fixes.explanation: God says the Egyptians “…will know that I am the LORD.” He says it again in verse 18, when He talks about being honored through Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen. That's the same promise twice, so I'd say He wants it heard. Pharaoh had brought a whole army, and God still said it plainly.

Right. Pharaoh “…took 600 of the best chariots, and all the other chariots of Egypt, with officers over all of them.” So the 600 were the best of the bunch, and the rest came along too. Every chariot of Egypt was in that line. That's a lot of chariots for one chase.

Nobody scatters in this verse. The Israelites “…were terrified and cried out to the LORD.” Then they speak to Moses. The text gives us fear and a cry, and nothing about running off in every direction.

They really say it: “…it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness.” They also remind Moses of what they'd said back in Egypt: “Leave us alone…” I think fear can make even slavery sound like the easy option. Moses answers in the next verse: “Do not be afraid.”

Close, but Moses says “be still,” not wait. The verse says they “…need only to be still.” I can see why wait comes to mind, since I stare at my oven timer like it owes me money. Still is the word Moses picks.
Busy isn't the word. Moses says they “…need only to be still.” Busy is more my style, with flour on my mustache and a timer going off every five minutes. Moses picks a different word for them.

God says the Israelites can “…go through the sea on dry ground.” The text says it again in verses 22 and 29, so it's worth noticing. Dry ground, with walls of water on the right and on the left. I'd have rubbed my eyes twice.
Muddy isn't the word. God says the Israelites can go through the sea “…on dry ground.” Verses 22 and 29 say it again. The text keeps saying dry, so I'll keep saying it too.

True. The angel of God, who had gone before the camp, went behind them, and the pillar of cloud stood behind them too. The text says it “…came between the camps of Egypt and Israel.” So the cloud sat right between the two camps. And “all night long neither camp went near the other.”

“…all that night the LORD drove back the sea with a strong east wind that turned it into dry land.” The wind blew all night long. Then the waters were divided, and the Israelites went through on dry ground. My chef's hat would not have survived that night.

No earthquake in this verse. The text says the LORD drove back the sea “…with a strong east wind…” and that went on all that night. Wind is the tool the text names. An earthquake is a fine guess, but this verse never mentions one.

The LORD “…caused their chariot wheels to wobble, so that they had difficulty driving.” Wobbly wheels are something anyone who has pushed a shopping cart can picture. Right after that, the Egyptians say, “…the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt!” The wheels were the problem, and the Egyptians noticed who was behind it.
Not the drivers. The text says He “…caused their chariot wheels to wobble…” and that's why they had difficulty driving. The wheels get the blame in the text. The drivers just get the difficulty.

The text doesn't say that. It says the waters covered the chariots and horsemen, “…the entire army of Pharaoh that had chased the Israelites into the sea.” Then it says, “Not one of them survived.” No one is named as an exception. This part is heavy, and the text doesn't soften it.

That's not in this song. Moses and the Israelites sing to the LORD about what He did to Pharaoh's army: “The horse and rider He has thrown into the sea.” The rock and the wilderness don't come up in these lines. This song is about the sea.

The song says, “Your right hand, O LORD, has shattered the enemy.” Notice the song stops talking about Him and starts talking straight to Him. The line right before it calls that hand “…majestic in power…” The word right hand shows up twice in one verse, so the song really wants us to look at His hand.

Moses did stretch out his hand over the sea (Exodus 14:21), but the song credits someone else. It says, “Your right hand, O LORD, has shattered the enemy.” The song points to the LORD's hand, not Moses's.

No swords from Israel in this part of the song. The only sword here is the enemy's, who says, “I will draw my sword…” (Exodus 15:9). The song says, “Your right hand, O LORD, has shattered the enemy.” The credit goes to the LORD.

The LORD leads the people He has redeemed, and the song names the goal: “…Your holy dwelling.” I think that tells us the journey doesn't end at the sea. Verse 17 adds more, calling it the mountain of His inheritance and the sanctuary His hands have established. That's where the song is headed.

The song doesn't name the Jordan. It says He will guide them “…to Your holy dwelling.” Verse 17 adds more, speaking of the mountain of His inheritance and the sanctuary His hands have established. The song points to His place, not a river.
Rest isn't the word. The song ends with “The LORD will reign forever and ever!” Reign is a king's word. The very last line is about His rule, and it has no end in it.

The text says Miriam the prophetess, Aaron's sister, “…took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women followed her with tambourines and dancing.” So the women are the ones who follow her. Then Miriam sings back to them. That's a lot of tambourines.
